The Bay of Broken Promises

By: Joy Summers | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Nelson Mandela Bay, despite interventions, ignores treasury, the SIU and the Auditor General warnings and its collapsing under its own rot

Unique Selling Point:
An unfolding drama that could lead to animal abuse, a money trail and corrupt officials

Summary:
THE FLASH POUND TENDER
When animals at their most vulnerable are used to make a quick buck, without any consideration of their welfare, the people behind it, grab our attention.
This time it’s a dodgy tender given in an emergency over Christmas to manage the pound, to a company with no experience, and a man that appears to be connected to Acting director Analisa Dyakala, the director of the Health Department, who has a history of handing out emergency contracts.

The SPCA have been warning for months that the contract had expired. For 50 years they have managed the pound on behalf of the municipality, then in January after a company called Busy Bee, with no experience was awarded the emergency contract for 6 months, Busy Bee evicted them from their offices. The SPCA was given 24 hours to vacate. They are currently in containers on the property still trying to help the animals that do come in, but that too will come to an end at the end of this week. They are frantically trying to raise money for a new property, but funds are well short of what they need, threatening the existence of the SPCA itself. Why would the municipality do that? Well it seems money and spite may be two drivers of their actions. The metro didn’t like the SPCA asking for its bills to be paid on time, and the ACTING HEALTH DIRECTOR Analise Dyakala may have seen a gap to make a quick buck. What she didn’t count on was the fury of the public at what is unfolding – which is already an animal welfare crisis.

Meanwhile two million rand allocated to build a new pound has disappeared and Dyakala told councilors in November she has no idea where the money went. But co-incidentally in August, Dyakala bought a new property for R2.5 million rand.

Even more suspicious is that a pitbull that was flagged by Darren Mann, the broadcaster who visited the pound, was taken to a small holding in Crockart’s hope, owned by Analisa Dyakala. Shots rang out and the pit bull has disappeared and the new owner of the pound Stanley Adam, apparently spent the night at this property. Critics are questioning whether a romantic relationship exists between these two people. But when questions are asked, about the competency, the impending animal welfare crisis and the deeply suspicious money trail, all that the municipality will say is that everything is above board and its confidential. These responses have infuriated the public who are simply not buying it.

The complete absence of transparency, the obvious question unanswered around what looks like a suspicious transaction is symptomatic of such a deep malaise of rot that hangs over this Metro.

With just over a million residents the R30 billion rand in unauthorized, irregular, wasteful expenditure is the largest in the country. It will be impossible for this money to be recovered.


Further information:
Things are so bad that the Nelson Mandela Bay Chamber of business is trying to create a kind of parallel structure to keep things going. Across every metric of what a city should provide the NMB officials are failing. Water, lighting, electricity, housing, roads and transport, safety.

The story of Nelson Mandela Bay has a stark narrative arc: millions of rands that vanish in untraceable irregular contracts at City Hall, resulting in national government withholding hundreds of millions of rands which ultimately leaves a mayor standing before residents trying to explain why they have no power of formal housing, a mayor who herself is facing an internal inquiry from the ANC integrity committee.

STAGGERING LOSSES IN WATER AND ELECTRICITY.
R368 million rand in water losses, and R1.2 billion in electricity losses.

RUSTING BUSSES, RUSTING TOWERS
Huge debt comes from the integrated public transport system which has largely collapsed and many of the busses and taxis purchased are rusting,

High voltage power lines also rotted from rust. Last month they fell over, even though they had been replaced 9 years ago but someone didn’t bother to add the wires. This collapse left large parts of the metro without power, and a water system unable to function. An official blamed gale force winds, until someone went to inspect the towers and discovered the truth.

In this metro, truth and accountability have disappeared with the missing files.

THE MISSING FILES
R2.6 billion rand has disappeared and is untraceable. Why? Because when the AG asked for files to find the money, an official removed those exact files from the cupboard, left them on the floor, and then a tap was turned on overnight on the floor above, flooding the basement and destroying the information. The AG is not buying this excuse, and neither is the opposition which has left the current CFO at the heart of this scandal drowning in excuses.

THE VEIL OF DARKNESS
10 000 streetlights don’t work leading to an increase in crime. SIU found the contracts from 2020 riddled with fraud and organized crime. Of the 198 broken street lights reported in 90 days, in Kariega – only two were repaired. New contracts to fix them awarded in late 2025 have faced immediate procedural and legal delays, but there are only four working trucks to fix them

ONE MAN AND A RAKE AND AN ENTIRE WATER TREATMENT PLANT
Footage filmed by Darren Mannn shows one man and a rake removing sanitary pads and condoms off a grate before sending the untreated sewerage into a local river.

THE EVERGREENS
R22 billion in Evergreen contracts just keep rolling over, some of these attached to city officials. The great drain heist, awarded in 2018, and surrounded by violent assassinations at the time is just one of them.


THE ANC HEAVY WEIGHT FACING CENSURE FROM HER OWN PARTY
Babalwa Lobishe, is the regional chairperson of the ANC. This heavy hitter promised to transform the city within her first 100 days as mayor in November 2024. But she has only managed to fix about 8 of the 85 service delivery items. Now Lobishe must explain to the ANC integrity committee why she tried to lease out a municipal transformer for R250 000 per month to a private company.

She is not the first. The former City manager has been sitting at home for years, and has earned over R7 million rand on suspension.

Meanwhile the City that became the subject of Crispian Olver’s book: How to steal a city, continues to regress. Olver had described syndicates of deeply entrenched networks of officials and businesspeople who used intimidation, legal threats and violence to protect their access to city funds. Eventually he had to flee the city to protect his safety. But his book on institutional decay suggests that this metro – far from reversing its decline has been unable to free itself from the grip of the officials stealing it blind. Investigations pile up at the SIU; Treasury refuses to hand out housing grants; the Auditor General throws up her hands in despair – citing missing documents, unaccounted funds and regression on all audit fronts.

The tiny glimmer of hope comes out of this metro. Its called the Erastyle case and a judgement at the Supreme court of appeal means that for the first time – officials in metro’s can be held accountable and made to pay back the money. This has already started happening. ( needs more research to find out exactly who and how much)

Script:


(Catherine Rice) These are the faces of the unwanted. The abandoned animals of the Nelson Mandela Bay Metro in the Eastern Cape. For more than 50 years, the SPCA has been stationed here in Kariega, contracted to look after the animals that are brought to the municipal pound on the one side, and their own on the other. But in December last year, that all changed. The municipality awarded an emergency tender to an unknown company to manage the pound.

(Deirdre Swift) There was no emergency. It leads you to believe that, possibly, there was some intent to put us at a disadvantage. So, for us, the emergency was created.

(Catherine Rice) And when the new company arrived in January, they gave the SPCA 24 hours to get out of the offices and the clinic. In desperation, they bundled into these containers. But even that is temporary and they’re urgently raising funds to buy a new base.

(Deirdre Swift) We're determined that the SPCA is not going to close its doors. Animal welfare is and will always remain our priority.

(Catherine Rice) But as we searched for answers on this story, we couldn’t ignore what we found… A city that appears to be abandoned by those in charge. And what is happening at the pound, may hint in part at how it got here.

(Catherine Rice) We’re on our way to the municipality’s pound in Kariega, and we’ve been through at least 20 robots – one after the other is not one working. And apparently, it’s been this way for years.

(Catherine Rice) Nelson Mandela Bay is choking on its own waste, drowning in debt, led by a mayor who’s under investigation for fraud and corruption.

(Daron Mann) Welcome to the Daron Mann Breakfast Show here on BayFM.

(Catherine Rice) Local broadcaster, Daron Mann, has been reporting on the city for the last 30 years.

(Daron Mann) More than 100,000 residents were without electricity as a result of a couple of pylons collapsing.

(Catherine Rice) He is an animal lover, and helps the SPCA when he can.

(Daron Mann) So, when this story broke… I mean, I was absolutely aghast. The public outrage at what has happened is entirely justified.

(Catherine Rice) What happened is that the municipality ignored the SPCA warnings last year that the contract to manage the pound was coming to an end. It lapsed and created a so-called emergency in December.

(Daron Mann) It falls over the Christmas break, and it was a 12-day period that the tender was open for. Now, we're talking about a city where it takes a year to get a pothole fixed. Business plans lie unattended for years, companies move elsewhere as a result. But in 12 days, we've now got this municipal pound tender done and dusted. There's one bidder…

(Catherine Rice) A company called Busy Bee won the tender. Busy Bee’s owner has worked with horses but has no prior experience running a pound.

(Deirdre Swift) You’re noisy. You’re noisy.

(Catherine Rice) Deirdre Swift is chairperson of the Kariega SPCA.

(Deirdre Swift) We’ve been doing this for years. We have never taken it for granted. We’ve always been awarded that contract because we have been the most qualified to actually do it.

(Catherine Rice) But the SPCA didn’t bid because they say the time frames were impossible. December is the worst month for animal cruelty, and their staff were on leave.

(Catherine Rice) How many days did you actually have to get your tender together?

(Deirdre Swift) Well, there was 11 days in total, six of those days were weekends and public holidays. It would have been impossible for us.

(Catherine Rice) The tender is to care for all livestock and domestic animals collected within the metro. But when we arrived, there was more livestock outside the pound than inside, and the clinic was closed.

(Daron Mann) I've been for a walkthrough: it's dismal. There's a clinic that is empty, doesn't function. There's not even a pen in it. There’s no medical supplies. There were no disinfectant trays between the various kennels.

(Catherine Rice) Busy Bee’s owner said he was contractually obliged to refer our request to the municipality when we asked for an interview. We sat down with the Mayoral Committee Member for Public Health, Thsonono Buyeye.

(Catherine Rice) Treasury clearly prohibits tenders being done during the Christmas period. How does the municipality justify ignoring Treasury's regulations?

(Thsonono Buyeye) We felt that we had no other option. It is not an unlawful thing to do but it is not advisable. We also understand that, maybe, there's going to be a question that says, “What emergency?”

(Catherine Rice) Well, that's the question. I mean, they requested information, asking “What's happening with the contract?”, for months. So, it seems to the public that this emergency was manufactured.

(Catherine Rice) Buyeye insisted that we didn’t have the context. He says the person responsible for the pound was off sick for almost a year and that caused the confusion.

(Catherine Rice) That still doesn't explain why the SPCA was not given an extension and was simply thrown off the property with 24 hours’ notice to vacate.

(Thsonono Buyeye) Once a contract expired, you could not extend an expired contract, it's unlawful.

(Catherine Rice) The money trail is not transparent. We know that the municipality allocated R750 000 to run the pound for six to nine months. A source alleges the money has been paid to Busy Bee. The MMC denies that.

(Thsonono Buyeye) As we are seated here, Catherine, Busy Bee has not been paid a cent.

(Catherine Rice) To add to the confusion, R2 million was allocated by the metro to upgrade the pound, but there’s a question mark around that money, too. And that leads us to Anna-Lisa Dyakala, the Acting Director of Public Health who was the final decision-maker on the pound tender.

(Catherine Rice) Last year, the Herald Newspaper reported that she didn’t know what had happened to the R2 million.

(Catherine Rice) What has happened to that R2 million?

(Tshonono Buyeye) The problem is that we were given money without plans. You need to plan before the money…

(Catherine Rice) But that money is missing?

(Thsonono Buyeye) No, that money is not missing. The money was taken away because it was not used by Public Health.

(Catherine Rice) Concerns still linger. The vet who was part of the bid originally has publicly distanced himself from Busy Bee, saying that the company didn’t meet his requirements. And why award a tender to a company that seems not able to fulfil its functions, leaving the very animals it’s supposed to protect vulnerable?

(Catherine Rice) You've described the municipal pound as fully functional. Do you stand by that?

(Tshonono Buyeye) We can't really now say that we are operating in a way we would like to be. We agree with you on that one.

(Catherine Rice) It’s not fully functional?

(Thsonono Buyeye) No, we agree because of a lot of infrastructure that SPCA has taken off site.

(Catherine Rice) So, it's the SPCA's fault?

(Thsonono Buyeye) No, it's not their fault. It's the municipality's fault of not making sure that we have all the infrastructure at the facility that is municipal-owned.

(Catherine Ricet) The SPCA deny they have removed any infrastructure. We also understand that the owner of Busy Bee has allegedly visited Dyakala at her home.

(Thsonono Buyeye) We know as a municipality that, on her spare time, she is a commercial farmer. It’s declared. She owns a number of cattle, horses, pigs, goats, sheep. She sells them.

(Catherine Rice) On top of her job?

(Thsonono Buyeye) Yes.

(Catherine Rice) She must be a very busy woman.

(Thsonono Buyeye) No, no. I am saying she’s here at work from Monday to Friday. She's responsible for cleaning the city, making sure that our beaches and everything is clean.

(Catherine Rice) And it’s here that two stories collide, providing the connection between the challenges faced by the SPCA and the decay we encountered on our visit.

(Catherine Rice) We were told that the owner of Busy Bee knows Dyakala via their mutual interest in farming, which is a small community here.

(Catherine Rice) But perhaps Dyakala is spending too much time farming. The city is a mess, and the metro is in crisis.

(Catherine Rice) Its unauthorised, fruitless and wasteful debt is almost R30 billion – three times higher than that of national government.

(Daron Mann) We will not survive another five years. That is not just my opinion. You speak to residents in this city and that's just the feeling. The current mayor and her team – they have to go.

(Mayor Babalwa Lobishe) Good afternoon metro residents…

(Catherine Rice) The mayor came in promising change. But it hasn’t happened; 60% of the city’s water isn’t being paid for, and electricity losses are over R1 billion and climbing. Ten thousand streetlights are broken, rusting pylons collapsed again this week leaving people without power, water treatment plants don’t work, drains are blocked for years. So, it wasn’t a surprise when Mayor Babalwa Lobishe cancelled our scheduled interview. Former Mayor Athol Trollip, now an MP, still lives in the Eastern Cape and laments the city he once tried to turn around.

(Athol Trollip) We’ve seen this revolving door of mayors.

(Catherine Rice) How many managers, mayors have there been in place?

(Athol Trollip) Well, 48 municipal managers since 2009. Now, that is completely alarming.

(Catherine Rice) Crazy!

(Athol Trollip) Six mayors in seven years. So, that's an indication of gross instability and chaotic revolving door of people becoming mayors and moving out and the next one.

(Catherine Rice) The direct consequence of that chaos is a dark, crime-ridden city.

(Athol Trollip) Well, Nelson Mandela Bay has become the crime city in the country – it has the highest crime rate. It is also probably the darkest metro city in South Africa. So, if people are being murdered and raped at night and it's dark and there's no streetlights, it will make you gloomy.

(Catherine Rice) But crime also flourishes inside the corridors of power. R2.6 billion has been spent with no documentation to record where the money has gone.

(Athol Trollip) In this city, when I was the Mayor, the most traumatised people I ever interacted with were the internal auditors. Their lives were threatened, their work was made completely untenable by documentation not being given. In Nelson Mandela Bay, you can’t account for the money, and the Auditor General knows that and so does Treasury. So, Treasury does not trust this city with funding.

(Catherine Rice) For years, corruption has strangled this metro’s progress. It has a qualified audit, and many of its legacy and emergency tenders are under investigation, which is why the recent rushed pound contract seems like such a bad idea. Meanwhile, the SPCA have until the end of the month before the municipality evicts them and their animals from the property.

(Deirdre Swift) Animals are not expendable. And welfare has been seriously, seriously compromised.

(Catherine Rice) On Friday, the Metro announced there is maintenance going on there, that they are committed to protecting animal welfare, and maintaining a safe hygienic and well-managed environment for all animals at the pound.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 15 March 2026 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: (Catherine Rice) These are the faces of the unwanted. The abandoned animals of the Nelson Mandela Bay Metro in the Eastern Cape. For more than 50 years, the SPCA has been stationed here in Kariega, contracted to look after the animals that are brought to the municipal pound on the one side, and their own on the other. But in December last year, that all changed. The municipality awarded an emergency tender to an unknown company to manage the pound. (Deirdre Swift) There was no emergency. It leads you to believe that, possibly, there was some intent to put us at a disadvantage. So, for us, the emergency was created. (Catherine Rice) And when the new company arrived in January, they gave the SPCA 24 hours to get out of the offices and the clinic. In desperation, they bundled into these containers. But even that is temporary and they’re urgently raising funds to buy a new base. (Deirdre Swift) We're determined that the SPCA is not going to close its doors. Animal welfare is and will always remain our priority. (Catherine Rice) But as we searched for answers on this story, we couldn’t ignore what we found… A city that appears to be abandoned by those in charge. And what is happening at the pound, may hint in part at how it got here. (Catherine Rice) We’re on our way to the municipality’s pound in Kariega, and we’ve been through at least 20 robots – one after the other is not one working. And apparently, it’s been this way for years. (Catherine Rice) Nelson Mandela Bay is choking on its own waste, drowning in debt, led by a mayor who’s under investigation for fraud and corruption. (Daron Mann) Welcome to the Daron Mann Breakfast Show here on BayFM. (Catherine Rice) Local broadcaster, Daron Mann, has been reporting on the city for the last 30 years. (Daron Mann) More than 100,000 residents were without electricity as a result of a couple of pylons collapsing. (Catherine Rice) He is an animal lover, and helps the SPCA when he can. (Daron Mann) So, when this story broke… I mean, I was absolutely aghast. The public outrage at what has happened is entirely justified. (Catherine Rice) What happened is that the municipality ignored the SPCA warnings last year that the contract to manage the pound was coming to an end. It lapsed and created a so-called emergency in December. (Daron Mann) It falls over the Christmas break, and it was a 12-day period that the tender was open for. Now, we're talking about a city where it takes a year to get a pothole fixed. Business plans lie unattended for years, companies move elsewhere as a result. But in 12 days, we've now got this municipal pound tender done and dusted. There's one bidder… (Catherine Rice) A company called Busy Bee won the tender. Busy Bee’s owner has worked with horses but has no prior experience running a pound. (Deirdre Swift) You’re noisy. You’re noisy. (Catherine Rice) Deirdre Swift is chairperson of the Kariega SPCA. (Deirdre Swift) We’ve been doing this for years. We have never taken it for granted. We’ve always been awarded that contract because we have been the most qualified to actually do it. (Catherine Rice) But the SPCA didn’t bid because they say the time frames were impossible. December is the worst month for animal cruelty, and their staff were on leave. (Catherine Rice) How many days did you actually have to get your tender together? (Deirdre Swift) Well, there was 11 days in total, six of those days were weekends and public holidays. It would have been impossible for us. (Catherine Rice) The tender is to care for all livestock and domestic animals collected within the metro. But when we arrived, there was more livestock outside the pound than inside, and the clinic was closed. (Daron Mann) I've been for a walkthrough: it's dismal. There's a clinic that is empty, doesn't function. There's not even a pen in it. There’s no medical supplies. There were no disinfectant trays between the various kennels. (Catherine Rice) Busy Bee’s owner said he was contractually obliged to refer our request to the municipality when we asked for an interview. We sat down with the Mayoral Committee Member for Public Health, Thsonono Buyeye. (Catherine Rice) Treasury clearly prohibits tenders being done during the Christmas period. How does the municipality justify ignoring Treasury's regulations? (Thsonono Buyeye) We felt that we had no other option. It is not an unlawful thing to do but it is not advisable. We also understand that, maybe, there's going to be a question that says, “What emergency?” (Catherine Rice) Well, that's the question. I mean, they requested information, asking “What's happening with the contract?”, for months. So, it seems to the public that this emergency was manufactured. (Catherine Rice) Buyeye insisted that we didn’t have the context. He says the person responsible for the pound was off sick for almost a year and that caused the confusion. (Catherine Rice) That still doesn't explain why the SPCA was not given an extension and was simply thrown off the property with 24 hours’ notice to vacate. (Thsonono Buyeye) Once a contract expired, you could not extend an expired contract, it's unlawful. (Catherine Rice) The money trail is not transparent. We know that the municipality allocated R750 000 to run the pound for six to nine months. A source alleges the money has been paid to Busy Bee. The MMC denies that. (Thsonono Buyeye) As we are seated here, Catherine, Busy Bee has not been paid a cent. (Catherine Rice) To add to the confusion, R2 million was allocated by the metro to upgrade the pound, but there’s a question mark around that money, too. And that leads us to Anna-Lisa Dyakala, the Acting Director of Public Health who was the final decision-maker on the pound tender. (Catherine Rice) Last year, the Herald Newspaper reported that she didn’t know what had happened to the R2 million. (Catherine Rice) What has happened to that R2 million? (Tshonono Buyeye) The problem is that we were given money without plans. You need to plan before the money… (Catherine Rice) But that money is missing? (Thsonono Buyeye) No, that money is not missing. The money was taken away because it was not used by Public Health. (Catherine Rice) Concerns still linger. The vet who was part of the bid originally has publicly distanced himself from Busy Bee, saying that the company didn’t meet his requirements. And why award a tender to a company that seems not able to fulfil its functions, leaving the very animals it’s supposed to protect vulnerable? (Catherine Rice) You've described the municipal pound as fully functional. Do you stand by that? (Tshonono Buyeye) We can't really now say that we are operating in a way we would like to be. We agree with you on that one. (Catherine Rice) It’s not fully functional? (Thsonono Buyeye) No, we agree because of a lot of infrastructure that SPCA has taken off site. (Catherine Rice) So, it's the SPCA's fault? (Thsonono Buyeye) No, it's not their fault. It's the municipality's fault of not making sure that we have all the infrastructure at the facility that is municipal-owned. (Catherine Ricet) The SPCA deny they have removed any infrastructure. We also understand that the owner of Busy Bee has allegedly visited Dyakala at her home. (Thsonono Buyeye) We know as a municipality that, on her spare time, she is a commercial farmer. It’s declared. She owns a number of cattle, horses, pigs, goats, sheep. She sells them. (Catherine Rice) On top of her job? (Thsonono Buyeye) Yes. (Catherine Rice) She must be a very busy woman. (Thsonono Buyeye) No, no. I am saying she’s here at work from Monday to Friday. She's responsible for cleaning the city, making sure that our beaches and everything is clean. (Catherine Rice) And it’s here that two stories collide, providing the connection between the challenges faced by the SPCA and the decay we encountered on our visit. (Catherine Rice) We were told that the owner of Busy Bee knows Dyakala via their mutual interest in farming, which is a small community here. (Catherine Rice) But perhaps Dyakala is spending too much time farming. The city is a mess, and the metro is in crisis. (Catherine Rice) Its unauthorised, fruitless and wasteful debt is almost R30 billion – three times higher than that of national government. (Daron Mann) We will not survive another five years. That is not just my opinion. You speak to residents in this city and that's just the feeling. The current mayor and her team – they have to go. (Mayor Babalwa Lobishe) Good afternoon metro residents… (Catherine Rice) The mayor came in promising change. But it hasn’t happened; 60% of the city’s water isn’t being paid for, and electricity losses are over R1 billion and climbing. Ten thousand streetlights are broken, rusting pylons collapsed again this week leaving people without power, water treatment plants don’t work, drains are blocked for years. So, it wasn’t a surprise when Mayor Babalwa Lobishe cancelled our scheduled interview. Former Mayor Athol Trollip, now an MP, still lives in the Eastern Cape and laments the city he once tried to turn around. (Athol Trollip) We’ve seen this revolving door of mayors. (Catherine Rice) How many managers, mayors have there been in place? (Athol Trollip) Well, 48 municipal managers since 2009. Now, that is completely alarming. (Catherine Rice) Crazy! (Athol Trollip) Six mayors in seven years. So, that's an indication of gross instability and chaotic revolving door of people becoming mayors and moving out and the next one. (Catherine Rice) The direct consequence of that chaos is a dark, crime-ridden city. (Athol Trollip) Well, Nelson Mandela Bay has become the crime city in the country – it has the highest crime rate. It is also probably the darkest metro city in South Africa. So, if people are being murdered and raped at night and it's dark and there's no streetlights, it will make you gloomy. (Catherine Rice) But crime also flourishes inside the corridors of power. R2.6 billion has been spent with no documentation to record where the money has gone. (Athol Trollip) In this city, when I was the Mayor, the most traumatised people I ever interacted with were the internal auditors. Their lives were threatened, their work was made completely untenable by documentation not being given. In Nelson Mandela Bay, you can’t account for the money, and the Auditor General knows that and so does Treasury. So, Treasury does not trust this city with funding. (Catherine Rice) For years, corruption has strangled this metro’s progress. It has a qualified audit, and many of its legacy and emergency tenders are under investigation, which is why the recent rushed pound contract seems like such a bad idea. Meanwhile, the SPCA have until the end of the month before the municipality evicts them and their animals from the property. (Deirdre Swift) Animals are not expendable. And welfare has been seriously, seriously compromised. (Catherine Rice) On Friday, the Metro announced there is maintenance going on there, that they are committed to protecting animal welfare, and maintaining a safe hygienic and well-managed environment for all animals at the pound.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Nelson Mandela Bay, despite interventions, ignores treasury, the SIU and the Auditor General warnings and its collapsing under its own rot
metadata.Unique Selling Point: An unfolding drama that could lead to animal abuse, a money trail and corrupt officials
metadata.Summary: THE FLASH POUND TENDER When animals at their most vulnerable are used to make a quick buck, without any consideration of their welfare, the people behind it, grab our attention. This time it’s a dodgy tender given in an emergency over Christmas to manage the pound, to a company with no experience, and a man that appears to be connected to Acting director Analisa Dyakala, the director of the Health Department, who has a history of handing out emergency contracts. The SPCA have been warning for months that the contract had expired. For 50 years they have managed the pound on behalf of the municipality, then in January after a company called Busy Bee, with no experience was awarded the emergency contract for 6 months, Busy Bee evicted them from their offices. The SPCA was given 24 hours to vacate. They are currently in containers on the property still trying to help the animals that do come in, but that too will come to an end at the end of this week. They are frantically trying to raise money for a new property, but funds are well short of what they need, threatening the existence of the SPCA itself. Why would the municipality do that? Well it seems money and spite may be two drivers of their actions. The metro didn’t like the SPCA asking for its bills to be paid on time, and the ACTING HEALTH DIRECTOR Analise Dyakala may have seen a gap to make a quick buck. What she didn’t count on was the fury of the public at what is unfolding – which is already an animal welfare crisis. Meanwhile two million rand allocated to build a new pound has disappeared and Dyakala told councilors in November she has no idea where the money went. But co-incidentally in August, Dyakala bought a new property for R2.5 million rand. Even more suspicious is that a pitbull that was flagged by Darren Mann, the broadcaster who visited the pound, was taken to a small holding in Crockart’s hope, owned by Analisa Dyakala. Shots rang out and the pit bull has disappeared and the new owner of the pound Stanley Adam, apparently spent the night at this property. Critics are questioning whether a romantic relationship exists between these two people. But when questions are asked, about the competency, the impending animal welfare crisis and the deeply suspicious money trail, all that the municipality will say is that everything is above board and its confidential. These responses have infuriated the public who are simply not buying it. The complete absence of transparency, the obvious question unanswered around what looks like a suspicious transaction is symptomatic of such a deep malaise of rot that hangs over this Metro. With just over a million residents the R30 billion rand in unauthorized, irregular, wasteful expenditure is the largest in the country. It will be impossible for this money to be recovered.
metadata.Further information: Things are so bad that the Nelson Mandela Bay Chamber of business is trying to create a kind of parallel structure to keep things going. Across every metric of what a city should provide the NMB officials are failing. Water, lighting, electricity, housing, roads and transport, safety. The story of Nelson Mandela Bay has a stark narrative arc: millions of rands that vanish in untraceable irregular contracts at City Hall, resulting in national government withholding hundreds of millions of rands which ultimately leaves a mayor standing before residents trying to explain why they have no power of formal housing, a mayor who herself is facing an internal inquiry from the ANC integrity committee. STAGGERING LOSSES IN WATER AND ELECTRICITY. R368 million rand in water losses, and R1.2 billion in electricity losses. RUSTING BUSSES, RUSTING TOWERS Huge debt comes from the integrated public transport system which has largely collapsed and many of the busses and taxis purchased are rusting, High voltage power lines also rotted from rust. Last month they fell over, even though they had been replaced 9 years ago but someone didn’t bother to add the wires. This collapse left large parts of the metro without power, and a water system unable to function. An official blamed gale force winds, until someone went to inspect the towers and discovered the truth. In this metro, truth and accountability have disappeared with the missing files. THE MISSING FILES R2.6 billion rand has disappeared and is untraceable. Why? Because when the AG asked for files to find the money, an official removed those exact files from the cupboard, left them on the floor, and then a tap was turned on overnight on the floor above, flooding the basement and destroying the information. The AG is not buying this excuse, and neither is the opposition which has left the current CFO at the heart of this scandal drowning in excuses. THE VEIL OF DARKNESS 10 000 streetlights don’t work leading to an increase in crime. SIU found the contracts from 2020 riddled with fraud and organized crime. Of the 198 broken street lights reported in 90 days, in Kariega – only two were repaired. New contracts to fix them awarded in late 2025 have faced immediate procedural and legal delays, but there are only four working trucks to fix them ONE MAN AND A RAKE AND AN ENTIRE WATER TREATMENT PLANT Footage filmed by Darren Mannn shows one man and a rake removing sanitary pads and condoms off a grate before sending the untreated sewerage into a local river. THE EVERGREENS R22 billion in Evergreen contracts just keep rolling over, some of these attached to city officials. The great drain heist, awarded in 2018, and surrounded by violent assassinations at the time is just one of them. THE ANC HEAVY WEIGHT FACING CENSURE FROM HER OWN PARTY Babalwa Lobishe, is the regional chairperson of the ANC. This heavy hitter promised to transform the city within her first 100 days as mayor in November 2024. But she has only managed to fix about 8 of the 85 service delivery items. Now Lobishe must explain to the ANC integrity committee why she tried to lease out a municipal transformer for R250 000 per month to a private company. She is not the first. The former City manager has been sitting at home for years, and has earned over R7 million rand on suspension. Meanwhile the City that became the subject of Crispian Olver’s book: How to steal a city, continues to regress. Olver had described syndicates of deeply entrenched networks of officials and businesspeople who used intimidation, legal threats and violence to protect their access to city funds. Eventually he had to flee the city to protect his safety. But his book on institutional decay suggests that this metro – far from reversing its decline has been unable to free itself from the grip of the officials stealing it blind. Investigations pile up at the SIU; Treasury refuses to hand out housing grants; the Auditor General throws up her hands in despair – citing missing documents, unaccounted funds and regression on all audit fronts. The tiny glimmer of hope comes out of this metro. Its called the Erastyle case and a judgement at the Supreme court of appeal means that for the first time – officials in metro’s can be held accountable and made to pay back the money. This has already started happening. ( needs more research to find out exactly who and how much)
